summary: The respondent demonstrates a sharp contrast between rigorous technical anticipation (modeling specific failure modes and synthetic edge cases) and a complete rejection of long-term macroscopic foresight due to startup survival pressures. Reflexivity is notably present through retrospective epistemic humility, as the CTO critiques the company's reliance on aggregate metrics and passive appendix reporting. Public engagement is absent in practice—relying entirely on downstream compliance with a city requirements document—which the respondent openly acknowledges as flawed. Finally, responsiveness is constrained by competitive procurement dynamics, where commercial pressures make adapting trajectories impossible without contractual and financial backing.
transcript:
Interview transcript P02 — Chief technology officer, AI perception startup
Case: Port Calder adaptive traffic signal and pedestrian detection system  |  SYNTHETIC DATA — not a real interview
[Interviewer] Your company supplied the detection models. How do you think about what could go wrong with them?
[Respondent] Constantly. That's most of my job. We model failure modes in a lot of detail — occlusion, low light, unusual gaits, people pushing strollers, cyclists dismounting. We built a whole synthetic test set for edge cases because the real data didn't have enough of them. If a detector misses a person in a wheelchair at dusk, that is a catastrophic failure for us, commercially and otherwise.
[Interviewer] Beyond detection accuracy — did you look at longer-term effects? How the system might change the street over five or ten years?
[Respondent] Honestly, no. We're a thirty-person company. Our runway is eighteen months. Ten-year urban effects is a question for someone with tenure. I don't say that dismissively, it's genuinely a different job from mine and I'm not equipped for it.
[Interviewer] Was there anyone in the consortium who did hold that question?
[Respondent] Not that I saw. There was a university partner on the original bid but they dropped out over funding. After that it was three vendors and the city. Everyone in the room was optimising their own deliverable.
[Interviewer] How did you decide what counted as acceptable performance?
[Respondent] The city gave us a target and we beat it. Ninety-eight point five on detection, we shipped at ninety-nine point one. Where it gets uncomfortable is that the aggregate number hides the distribution. Our worst subgroup was people using mobility aids, and that number was materially lower. We flagged it, we put it in the report, and then — nobody asked about it, and we moved on. In hindsight flagging it in an appendix isn't the same as raising it.
[Interviewer] Did you speak to any disability organisations directly?
[Respondent] No. We had the city's requirements document and we built to it. In retrospect that's a strange way to build something that has to detect people, isn't it — we never met any of the people the system was hardest for.
[Interviewer] What would have had to be different for that to happen?
[Respondent] Someone would have had to put it in the contract and pay for it. I know how that sounds. But we bid against two other firms on price. If I'd priced in a user research programme we wouldn't have won, and then you'd be interviewing whoever did.
